TODAY IN NAVAL HISTORY

1826

While engaging in the pursuit of mutineers from the American whaling ship Globe, the schooner Dolphin under the command of Lieutenant John Percival arrives at Honolulu. It becomes the first American warship to visit the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii).

1861

The U.S. steamer Star of the West, carrying reinforcements destined for Fort Sumter, arrives off Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, and takes fire from Confederate forces at Fort Moultrie and Morris Island. This marks the first shots fired at a vessel flying the American flag during the Civil War.

1942

Five German U-boats commence Operation Drumbeat off the East Coast of the United States, sinking 26 Allied ships over the next month.

1945

Task Force 77, under Admiral Thomas C. Kinkaid, supported by naval gunfire and carrier aircraft, lands Army troops at Lingayen Gulf, Philippines. Kamikazes descend on the invasion force, hitting four ships, including the battleship Mississippi (BB-41). For days, suicide aircraft continue to plague the ships supporting the landings, which are also attacked by Japanese assault demolition boats.

1980

LCDR Gaylord Parrett, Jr., USNA '65, USN and ENS Dewayne Cousin '79, USN were lost when the TA-4J Skyhawk they were aboard crashed into the Pacific Ocean southwest of San Diego, California. Parrett was son of a 1944 USNA alumnus; following graduation he attended flight school and deployed twice to Vietnam. He was survived by his wife, son and parents. Cousin was a native of Lawton, Oklahoma, where he was an active member of the high school ROTC. It seems he was temporarily assigned to Composite Squadron (VC) 7 before starting flight training. He was survived by his mother, four brothers and eight sisters.

The end.

data.text:
The heavy oak door of the officers’ mess swung open, and the hum of conversation inside instantly died. Dozens of men in pressed olive wool uniforms sat at white-clothed tables, their silver forks hovering halfway to their mouths. They were captains, majors, and colonels of the United States Army, men trained to lead soldiers into the chaos of war with unwavering voices. Yet, in the presence of one man, they lost the ability to speak.
Benjamin O. Davis Sr. paused in the doorway. He adjusted his cap, his movements slow and deliberate. He scanned the room, his eyes passing over faces that turned away or studied their dinner plates with sudden, intense interest. There was no shouting. There were no slurs hurled across the room. There was only a vacuum of sound, a suffocating bubble of isolation that moved with him wherever he walked.
He moved to a small table in the corner, the one that was always empty. He pulled out his chair, sat down, and unfolded his napkin. The noise in the room slowly returned, but it was a low, guarded murmur, distinct from the boisterous laughter that had filled the air moments before. He was a commissioned officer in the service of his country. He wore the same insignia and followed the same regulations. But to the men around him, he was an error in the system that refused to be corrected.
He signaled the steward for coffee. He did not look up. He knew that if he made eye contact, he would force a confrontation that the Army would blame him for causing.
For nearly fifty years, this was his daily reality. Benjamin O. Davis Sr. was not fighting a foreign enemy on a distant battlefield. He was fighting a war of attrition against his own colleagues, a battle fought not with bullets, but with silence. He had chosen a career where his very existence was considered an impossibility, and for five decades, he refused to let them pretend he wasn't there.
The stakes were far higher than his own comfort or career advancement. He understood that he was a placeholder for an entire race. If he lost his temper, if he failed a single inspection, or if he resigned in bitterness, the narrative would be set in stone for generations. The critics would say that a Black man lacked the temperament for command. They would say the experiment had failed. If this man walked away, the door behind him would be locked and bolted.
The path he walked was narrow and lined with traps. He had enlisted in the brief fervor of the Spanish-American War in 1898, serving initially as a temporary lieutenant in an all-Black volunteer unit. When that force was disbanded, he did the unthinkable: he enlisted as a private in the regular Army, determined to climb the ladder from the bottom rung. He was a soldier in a military that did not want him, serving a country that did not fully claim him.
By 1901, he had passed the rigorous examinations to become a second lieutenant in the regular Army. It was a feat of intellectual and physical excellence that should have been celebrated. Instead, it created a bureaucratic crisis. He was sent to the Philippines, then to Wyoming, but always with a caveat. He could not be placed in a position where he might outrank a white officer.
The United States Army was built on a foundation of absolute hierarchy and discipline. The logic stated that a fighting force relied on the unquestioned authority of its leaders. Military doctrine held that social cohesion was essential for unit morale and effectiveness. Segregation was enforced not merely as prejudice, but as a strategic necessity to prevent internal conflict. The system prioritized the comfort of the majority over the rights of the individual. This rule works — until it meets this person.
The rupture in the system was rarely loud; it was often quiet and administrative. It happened when Davis was assigned to duty at a new post. He would arrive, his uniform impeccable, his orders in hand. He would present himself to the commanding officer, offering a sharp salute.
The return salute would come, but it was mechanical. The handshake was often omitted. The invitation to the officers’ club social on Friday night—a standard courtesy extended to every new arrival—never materialized.
Davis would return to his quarters, where his wife awaited him. She would look at his face and know. There would be no welcome dinner. There would be no bridge games with the other couples. They were on an island. He would remove his jacket, hang it carefully, and sit in the crushing quiet of a house that the neighbors ignored. It was a social death, repeated every few years, in every new town.
This was the fracture point. A lesser man would have screamed. A weaker man would have requested a transfer to a civilian life where he could be respected. Davis simply polished his boots. He understood that his punishment for excellence was invisibility.
The struggle stretched over decades, turning into a grinding test of endurance. The Army solved the "Davis Problem" by shuffling him to the few posts where his rank would not cause friction. He was sent to Liberia as a military attaché. He was assigned to Tuskegee Institute and Wilberforce University to teach military tactics to students. He was kept away from the main body of the Army, hidden in the margins of the map.
Yet, even in exile, he maintained a standard of perfection that bordered on obsession. When he was inspected, his records were flawless. When he drilled troops, they were sharper than the white units stationed miles away. He knew that he was being watched through a microscope, and he denied his detractors even a speck of dust to criticize.
His son, Benjamin O. Davis Jr., watched this silent struggle from the sidelines. He saw his father’s stoicism. He saw the way his father commanded respect by refusing to demand it. When the younger Davis entered West Point in 1932, he was subjected to "The Silence"—an organized campaign where no cadet spoke to him outside the line of duty for four entire years. He survived it because he had watched his father survive it for thirty.
The father’s career seemed destined to end in a quiet retirement as a colonel. By 1940, with war looming in Europe, Davis was nearing the mandatory retirement age. The system had successfully contained him. He had served honorably, but the glass ceiling remained intact. He had been a good soldier, but the Army was not ready for a Black general.
But the world was changing. The pressure was building outside the gates. The Black press, civil rights organizations, and political leaders began to ask why a man with forty years of flawless service was stalled in rank. The hypocrisy of fighting a war against tyranny abroad while enforcing a caste system at home was becoming a strategic liability.
In October 1940, the order came from the White House. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, facing an election and growing pressure, promoted Benjamin O. Davis Sr. to Brigadier General.
The news rippled through the War Department. It was a shock to the system. For the first time in the history of the United States, a Black man wore the star of a general.
The promotion did not magically erase the prejudice. General Davis was still often relegated to inspection tours and public relations roles, aimed at boosting morale among Black troops rather than commanding divisions in combat. But the symbol was undeniable. When he walked onto a base now, the salute was not just a courtesy; it was a requirement directed at a general officer.
He used his new rank to methodically dismantle the system that had tried to silence him. He served on the Advisory Committee on Negro Troop Policies. He traveled to the European theater, interviewing soldiers, documenting discrimination, and writing reports that landed on the desks of the highest commanders. He did not use emotional language. He used the Army’s own logic against it. He argued that segregation was inefficient. He proved that it wasted manpower and hampered the war effort.
He retired in 1948, exactly fifty years after he first enlisted. Six days after his retirement ceremony, President Harry Truman signed Executive Order 9981, abolishing racial discrimination in the armed forces.
The timing was not a coincidence. The reports Davis wrote, the example he set, and the sheer irrefutable fact of his competence had eroded the foundation of segregation until it collapsed.
General Benjamin O. Davis Sr. died in 1970. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. He did not lead a charge up a hill under enemy fire. He did not capture a city. His bravery was found in the fifty years of dinners eaten alone. It was found in the thousands of mornings he put on a uniform that represented a country that did not want him, and dared them to tell him he didn't belong.
He proved that the loudest way to change the world is sometimes just to stay in the room.
Sources: Benjamin O. Davis, Jr.: American: An Autobiography; U.S. Army Center of Military History; "America's First Black General" by Marvin E. Fletcher.
